title: When might a database ignore an index (functions on columns, leading wildcard, small tables, low selectivity, large result sets)?
shortTitle: When might a database ignore an index — functions on columns, leading wildcard, small tables, low selectivity, large result sets

s1_definition.profdef: The optimizer ignores an existing index when using it would be slower or impossible. Common causes are a non-sargable predicate that wraps the indexed column in a function or applies a leading wildcard, a table so small that a full scan is cheaper than tree navigation, a predicate with low selectivity that matches most rows, a result set so large that random index lookups cost more than a sequential scan, implicit type coercion that defeats matching, and stale statistics that mislead the cost estimate.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India clerk skips the index thumb-tabs in several situations. If you ask "find accounts where the uppercased name equals RAJESH," the clerk cannot use the alphabetical tabs because the tabs are sorted by the original name, not the transformed one. If you search for "any name containing kumar" with the wildcard at the front, the tabs are useless because they sort by first letter. If the ledger has only ten accounts, flipping through all ten is faster than consulting the index. If nearly every account is ACTIVE, an index on status matches almost everyone, so reading the whole ledger is simpler. And if your query returns eighty percent of rows anyway, jumping back and forth to the index for each one is slower than reading straight through.
s1_definition.oneliner: The database ignores an index when a function hides the column, a leading wildcard breaks ordering, the table is tiny, the predicate is unselective, or the result set is huge.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The optimizer ignores an existing index when using it would be slower or impossible. Common causes are a non-sargable predicate that wraps the indexed column in a function or applies a leading wildcard, a table so small that a full scan is cheaper than tree navigation, a predicate with low selectivity that matches most rows, a result set so large that random index lookups cost more than a sequential scan, implicit type coercion that defeats matching, and stale statistics that mislead the cost estimate.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India clerk skips the index thumb-tabs in several situations. If you ask "find accounts where the uppercased name equals RAJESH," the clerk cannot use the alphabetical tabs because the tabs are sorted by the original name, not the transformed one. If you search for "any name containing kumar" with the wildcard at the front, the tabs are useless because they sort by first letter. If the ledger has only ten accounts, flipping through all ten is faster than consulting the index. If nearly every account is ACTIVE, an index on status matches almost everyone, so reading the whole ledger is simpler. And if your query returns eighty percent of rows anyway, jumping back and forth to the index for each one is slower than reading straight through.

**One line to remember:** The database ignores an index when a function hides the column, a leading wildcard breaks ordering, the table is tiny, the predicate is unselective, or the result set is huge.

sections.s2_technical:
The most common cause is a function on the indexed column, which makes the predicate non-sargable. `WHERE UPPER(email) = 'RAJESH@BANK.IN'` or `WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026` forces the engine to compute the function on every row, so the B+tree ordering on the raw column is useless and it falls back to a scan. The fix is to rewrite as a range on the raw column, or to build an expression index on the exact function.

A leading wildcard like `WHERE name LIKE '%kumar'` cannot use a normal B+tree because the tree is sorted left to right; there is no known prefix to seek to. A trailing wildcard like `LIKE 'Raj%'` works fine because it fixes the prefix. For leading-wildcard search banks use full-text indexes or trigram indexes instead.

A small table is often faster to scan entirely. If a lookup table has fifty rows that all fit in one page, reading that single page beats descending a tree and doing a bookmark lookup, so the planner picks a sequential scan even though an index exists.

Low selectivity means the predicate matches a large fraction of rows. An index on a status column where ninety-five percent of accounts are ACTIVE is nearly useless for `WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'`, because the engine would do millions of random index lookups to return almost everything; a sequential scan is cheaper. Indexes help most on high-selectivity columns.

A large result set triggers the same reasoning even on a selective-looking predicate: if a range returns most of the table, random heap fetches via the index cost more than one sequential pass. The optimizer's crossover point is typically a few percent of the table.

Two more causes: implicit type coercion, such as comparing an indexed `VARCHAR` column to a numeric literal, can force a cast on the column and defeat the index; and stale statistics can make the planner badly misjudge selectivity. A senior nuance is to confirm every suspicion with the execution plan — a "Seq Scan" where you expected an "Index Scan" is the signal to investigate.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A developer wrote the login lookup as `WHERE UPPER(email) = ?`. Logins got slow at scale because this function predicate made the email index unusable. This is exactly the function-on-column case, fixed by a case-insensitive expression index or by normalizing the stored value.

Problem 2 — The support search "find customers whose name ends in Kumar" uses a leading wildcard and ignores the name index. This is exactly the leading-wildcard case, fixed with a trigram or full-text index.

Problem 3 — A report filters `WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'` where almost all accounts are active. The planner ignores the status index because it is unselective. This is exactly the low-selectivity case; a partial index on the rare INACTIVE rows is the real fix.

The mini-project builds an account search service that demonstrates a bad function predicate and its sargable rewrite, a leading-wildcard search and its trigram alternative, and an unselective status filter. It logs the plan each time.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/index-ignore-service-1.0.0.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev

# Prove the function defeats the plain index (Seq Scan)
psql -d bankdb -c "EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE UPPER(email)=UPPER('rajesh@bank.in');"

# Prove the expression index is used (Index Scan on ix_email_lower)
psql -d bankdb -c "EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE LOWER(email)=LOWER('rajesh@bank.in');"

# Prove the trigram index serves leading wildcard
psql -d bankdb -c "EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE holder_name ILIKE '%kumar';"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a bad login lookup `WHERE UPPER(email) = 'RAJESH@BANK.IN'`, then its fixed version, then a leading-wildcard name search.

Step 1 — The bad query applies `UPPER()` to the email column of every row. Because the plain index `ix_email` is sorted by the raw email value, not the uppercased value, the planner cannot use it and chooses a sequential scan over all rows.

Step 2 — We rewrite to `LOWER(email) = LOWER(?)`. Now the predicate exactly matches the expression index `ix_email_lower`, which stores the lowercased values in sorted order, so the planner performs an index scan and jumps straight to Rajesh.

Step 3 — The name search uses a leading wildcard `%kumar`. The ordinary name index is ignored because there is no fixed prefix to seek. The trigram index `ix_name_trgm` breaks names into three-character fragments, so it can match the fragment and find Rajesh Kumar.

Step 4 — A status filter `WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'` would match almost every row, so the planner ignores any status index and scans; the partial index on the rare non-active rows is what actually helps there.

Step 5 — Each fixed query returns the matching accounts quickly, and the plan confirms an index scan rather than a sequential scan.

```text
2026-10-25 14:12:04 INFO  AccountSearchService - Searching by email using LOWER() expression index ix_email_lower
2026-10-25 14:12:04 INFO  AccountSearchService - Leading-wildcard name search '%kumar%' uses trigram index ix_name_trgm
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  BAD: WHERE UPPER(email)=?            GOOD: WHERE LOWER(email)=?
    │ function hides column             │ matches expression index
    ▼                                   ▼
  ix_email IGNORED → Seq Scan         ix_email_lower → Index Scan
    │ reads all rows                    │ seek to one key
    ▼                                   ▼
  slow                                fast

  LEADING WILDCARD: name ILIKE '%kumar'      LOW SELECTIVITY: status='ACTIVE'
    │ no fixed prefix                          │ matches 95% of rows
    ▼                                          ▼
  normal index IGNORED → trigram ix_name_trgm  status index IGNORED → Seq Scan
                                               (partial index on INACTIVE helps)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A database ignores an existing index whenever using it would be slower or simply impossible, and the optimizer makes that call on cost. The most frequent reason is a non-sargable predicate: wrapping the indexed column in a function like UPPER or YEAR, or using a leading wildcard such as LIKE percent-kumar, hides the column's natural order so the B-tree cannot be seeked. The other reasons are a table small enough that a full scan beats tree navigation, a predicate with low selectivity that matches most of the rows, a result set so large that random index lookups cost more than one sequential pass, implicit type coercion that forces a cast on the column, and stale statistics that mislead the estimate.

The fixes follow directly from the cause. For a function on a column I either rewrite it as a sargable range on the raw column, or I build an expression index that matches the exact function. For a leading wildcard I use a trigram or full-text index instead of a normal B-tree. For a low-selectivity column I use a partial index on the rare value that people actually search for. And for small tables I simply accept the scan, because it is genuinely faster.

At the National Bank of India this came up with our login lookup, which someone had written as WHERE UPPER of email equals the input. It worked in testing but crawled in production because the function defeated the email index and every login did a full scan. I added an expression index on LOWER of email and rewrote the query to match it, and logins went back to a single index seek. Separately, a support search for names ending in Kumar used a leading wildcard, so I added a trigram index to make that pattern fast.

The discipline I always stress is to confirm the behavior with the execution plan rather than assuming. A Sequential Scan where I expected an Index Scan is the exact signal that a function, a wildcard, selectivity, or stale statistics is defeating my index, and I run EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after every fix.
